title: ScaffoldSwap: Are Discrete Speech Units Necessary as a Temporal Scaffold for Audio-Driven 3D Facial Animation?

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to isolate the effect of speech representation on 3D facial animation quality by controlled comparison. None of the prior papers explicitly aim to isolate the effect of speech representation on animation quality in a controlled manner. While papers like [1], [2], [3], [6], and [7] address speech-driven 3D facial animation, their focus is on synthesis methods, expressiveness, or style control rather than isolating the impact of speech representation itself. Papers like [8] and [16] compare discrete and continuous speech features but do so in the context of ASR, TTS, or SpeechLLMs, not 3D facial animation.

### Mechanism
The contribution uses ScaffoldSwap ablation comparing three speech conditioning approaches (continuous SSL features, discrete speech units, and phoneme+timing) under identical experimental conditions. Paper [8] conducts a comparative analysis of discrete and continuous SSL features under controlled settings, but it focuses on spoken language understanding tasks rather than 3D facial animation. Paper [16] also compares discrete tokens and continuous features but in the context of ASR and TTS. Neither paper applies this mechanism to 3D facial animation or uses the specific ScaffoldSwap ablation design described here. No prior paper matches the mechanism cross-domain.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves systematic comparison on BIWI and VOCASET using Lip Vertex Error (LVE) across three seeds. Papers [1], [2], [3], [6], and [7] evaluate speech-driven 3D facial animation but do not use LVE or the specific benchmark datasets BIWI and VOCASET. Paper [8] uses a controlled comparison design but applies it to ASR and TTS tasks, not 3D facial animation. No prior paper uses the same evaluation design (benchmark family, metric semantics, or validation framework).

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of audio-driven 3D facial animation / speech conditioning. Papers [1], [2], [3], [6], and [7] all work in the same general application area of speech-driven 3D facial animation, even though they target different sub-problems (e.g., expressiveness, style control, disentanglement). This domain is well-covered by prior work.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to determine whether discretization itself (not the underlying representation) drives gains. None of the prior papers explicitly report or establish this specific empirical relationship. While several papers discuss discrete representations (e.g., [10], [13], [15], [27]), they focus on different aspects, such as information completeness, tone distinctions, or pre-training optimization, rather than isolating the effect of discretization itself as the driver of performance gains. No prior paper establishes the same relationship between discretization and performance gains.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves an ablation comparing discrete units (HuBERT + k-means) against HuBERT-continuous (same encoder without k-means quantization). Papers such as [25] (vq-wav2vec) and [27] (Do Discrete Self-Supervised Representations of Speech Capture Tone Distinctions?) use k-means clustering for discretization in speech representations, and [10] (RepCodec) discusses discrete speech tokenization. However, none of these papers perform the specific ablation comparing discrete versus continuous representations within the same encoder to isolate the effect of discretization itself. Thus, the mechanism is uncovered.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design compares discrete units against continuous representations using metrics like LVE and statistical significance tests. Papers such as [13] (Estimating the Completeness of Discrete Speech Units) and [27] (Do Discrete Self-Supervised Representations of Speech Capture Tone Distinctions?) use similar evaluation designs, including statistical comparisons of discrete representations. While the specific benchmarks and metrics differ, the evaluation design (comparing discrete versus continuous representations with statistical significance tests) is substantively equivalent. Therefore, the evaluation facet is covered.

### Domain
The domain is discrete speech tokenization and information bottleneck analysis. Papers such as [10] (RepCodec), [25] (vq-wav2vec), and [27] (Do Discrete Self-Supervised Representations of Speech Capture Tone Distinctions?) all operate in the same general application area of discrete speech tokenization and representation learning. Although the specific sub-problems differ, the domain is covered.

### Purpose
The purpose of the contribution is to assess whether explicit timing features add value beyond frame-level phoneme identity. None of the prior papers explicitly report or establish this specific empirical relationship. While several papers (e.g., [13], [15], [21], [23]) discuss duration modeling or timing features in speech recognition or synthesis, they do not address the comparative value of timing features versus phoneme identity in lip-sync conditioning. Therefore, no prior paper covers this purpose.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves ablating within-phoneme position and duration features from the phoneme+timing condition (Condition C). Ablation experiments are a common analysis protocol, and [22] explicitly describes randomized ablation for feature importance, which matches the design-level equivalence of the mechanism. Although [22] applies ablation to a different domain (general feature importance in predictive models), the primitive of ablating features to measure their contribution is substantively equivalent.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves measuring changes in LVE (Lip Velocity Error) and conducting a temporal-shuffle sanity check. While the specific LVE metric and shuffle protocol are new, the evaluation design broadly aligns with standard ablation-based validation setups seen in [22] and permutation-based tests described in [27] and [28]. These papers use similar statistical frameworks to assess feature importance or experimental reliability. Thus, the evaluation design is covered.

### Domain
The domain is phoneme-based lip-sync conditioning. Several prior papers ([2], [5], [6], [8], [17], [25]) address lip-sync or phoneme-based conditioning in speech-driven animation or synthesis. While the specific sub-problem of timing features versus phoneme identity is new, the general application area of phoneme-based lip-sync is well-covered.
